item.title: Marvel’s X-Men movie has found its Angel in Asa Germann, best known for his roles in Gen V and Scream 7.
item.description:
Marvel’s X-Men movie has found its Angel in Asa Germann, best known for his roles in Gen V and Scream 7.
As per The Hollywood Reporter, Germann had actually auditioned for the part of Cyclops, which eventually went to Kit Connor. He wasn’t out of the running, though, and is now playing the X-Men’s iconic Warren Worthington III (better known by his nickname, Angel).
At 28 years old, Germann joins the ranks of a cast that trends younger, alongside 24-year-old Sadie Sink (Jean Gray), 23-year-old Maya Boyd (Storm), and 25-year-old Inde Navarrette, who was confirmed to play Rogue at Disney’s D23 fan convention last month.
Other confirmed cast members include Samara Weaving as Emma Frost and Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, with Adam Driver set to play the part of villain Mister Sinister.
THR states that, although Germann didn’t nab Cyclops, Marvel Studios was so impressed with his audition that they decided to cast him as Angel. This isn't totally new territory for the actor; he’s quite familiar with superhero universes, having played Sam Riordan in The Boys spin-off show Gen V, a character with superhuman strength, stamina, mobility, and hearing, among other traits.
Angel's superpowers are all avian-related, given his wings and all. The character has been a popular topic on social media as of late, with fans remembering a harrowing scene from 2006's X-Men: The Last Stand where he pulled out his feathers as a child.
First appearing in 1963 comic The X-Men #1, Angel was a founding member of the X-Men and an heir to the wealthy Worthington estate. He operated as a vigilante under the name Avenging Angel before joining the group, eventually getting transformed into the brooding Archangel with metallic wings by the hand of Apocalypse.
Marvel's X-Men cast continues to roll out as the months go by, something that Marvel Studios prez Kevin Feige said would happen at D23. By the looks of things, this cast is here to stay, as Feige teased "sagas upon sagas" of stories about the X-Men that "haven't been told" yet.
"Having 85, almost 90 years of comic book history, there's so many stories yet to tell," Feige said. "We announced a very young, new cast for a property called X-Men the other day. And that's great, because there's been 10 great X-Men movies [but] there can be 100 more," he said at D23's Disney Worldbuilers panel.
Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze.

item.title: Wardogs has already surpassed a million copies sold and is lighting up Steam's concurrent player charts.
item.description:
Wardogs has already surpassed a million copies sold and is lighting up Steam's concurrent player charts.
Earlier today, developer Bulkhead launched its brand new all-out warfare FPS, Wardogs. The game has been one of the more highly anticipated shooters of this year and players are showing up for it in force. According to the developer, the game has already surpassed a million copies sold, and SteamDB shows that the game has over 300,000 concurrent players. As a result, a lot of players are being put into server queues, preventing them from getting directly into the action.
“To cross a million copies sold as we launch into early access is mental,” said Joe Brammer, CEO at Bulkhead. “We've spent the last few months showing people exactly what Wardogs is, what it isn't, and at one point literally gave everyone ten reasons not to buy it. We didn't want people buying into blind hype. So seeing more than one million people choose to jump in and play the game at early access launch means a huge amount to all of us. But this is still early access. We've got things to fix, things we want to improve and a lot more we want to build. The best thing players can do now is keep playing, keep telling us what they think and keep giving us those ridiculous Wardogs moments.”
Wardogs is currently only available on PC, making its debut sales numbers all the more impressive, but it is coming to consoles. Bulkhead confirmed that Wardogs is targeting a 2028 release for PS5 and Xbox, but didn't offer a concrete release date. The developer has also noted that it expects the hype to die down eventually, as they plan to take their time when it comes to releasing new content and therefore there may be drops in player counts.
However, it's a strong debut from a new multiplayer shooter. Whether the game can keep players interested to keep returning as new content is added remains to be seen, but it's great to have something other than Call of Duty and Battlefield making an impact. Wardogs attempts to find a unique balance between mil-sims like Arma and something a bit more casual like Battlefield, resulting in a tense, grounded, but large-scale experience filled with emergent moments. So far, players seem to be eating it up and it will likely only continue to grow its audience as word of mouth spreads.
Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

item.title: Dead or Alive 6 Last Round Project Manager Tsuyoshi Iuchi has sparked a debate within the fighting game community after explaining why the team at Koei Tecmo is dialing back on making sexy costumes.
item.description:
Dead or Alive 6 Last Round Project Manager Tsuyoshi Iuchi has sparked a debate within the fighting game community after explaining why the team at Koei Tecmo is dialing back on making sexy costumes.
Dead or Alive is a fighting game franchise with a fiercely loyal fanbase and a dedicated competitive scene. Despite these factors, it’s also known as the fighting game series with the most fanservice — a label that’s hard to get away from, given the jiggle physics, dating-sim-heavy spinoff games, and sexy outfits that exist in abundance in almost every DoA title.
While Dead or Alive 7 is in active development, DoA 6 Last Round is still getting content, including a new character that was just announced yesterday. Minato’s addition to the roster hasn’t come without controversy; some fans are accusing the schoolgirl of being a copy/paste of Honoka, while others are pointing toward a September 9 Famitsu interview that included some divisive remarks from the game’s development team.
Of these remarks, one is standing out from the rest: Project Manager Tsuyoshi Iuchi confirmed that Koei Tecmo is making the decision to step back from making more sexy outfits for Dead or Alive’s characters. This is a big change for the franchise, and one that’s been met with backlash and confusion from its fanbase.
The reason for this, Iuchi says, is because players are "embarrassed" to use such costumes when playing competitively. (This isn’t a huge surprise; swimsuit-style costumes for female characters have been banned or restricted at numerous esports tournaments across several different fighting games over the years.)
“I understand that some people are hoping for sexy costumes, but actually, sexy costumes tend to be used less frequently in competitive games due to embarrassment and other factors. For example, even in ranked matches, you don't often see your opponents wearing swimsuit costumes, right? This time, we're aiming for costumes that ‘people who like that character will continue to use,’ so the sexy elements are naturally kept to a minimum,” he said.
That’s not the only comment that’s catching players’ eyes; Director Akihiro Nakamura also responded to Famitsu’s question regarding Minato’s moveset, which the outlet noted was strikingly similar to Honoka’s.
“While they both use the same techniques, the key difference lies in their backstory: Honoka has an innate ability to instantly imitate any technique she sees, while Minato learns by studying through a device and through hard work,” he explained. “Additionally, Honoka enjoys watching martial arts and professional wrestling, so she chooses techniques she likes as a hobby, whereas Minato learns techniques with the visual appeal and enjoyment of dance in mind.”
This answer, combined with team's decision to slow down on sexy costumes, has left the DoA community equal parts frustrated and disappointed, leading to a wave of backlash from players online.
“What did we expect?” one fan wrote on X. “They don't care about the fans or the game. They want to shake a couple of more dollars out of the community with bare-minimum effort. I can already see DOA7 not having crossplay or rollback [netcode] and Koei saying, ‘$80 bucks, please.’”
“What happens when Minato fights Honoka? Is she going to steal her stolen moves, too?” prominent community member Emery Reigns said.
Even Japanese players aren’t happy with Minato’s moveset, with one writing, "Another cash grab? I shelled out for 6, but I can barely carry anything over, can't even change my hair color let alone power up — it's actually worse off, isn't it? Way too disappointing.”
Guess its more Dead than Alive
What happens when Minato fights Honoka? She going to steal her stolen moves too? 😂😂😂😂 pic.twitter.com/LaDPbpvV5m
Team Ninja and Koei Tecmo have mugged off the Dead or Alive player base beyond belief. Please read this shit. pic.twitter.com/bFiivxq1v9
Dead or Alive 7 is still being developed, and it doesn’t have a release date at the time of writing. Dead or Alive 6 Last Round received middling reviews on its release in June, with many players — and even our own reviewers at IGN — bemoaning the lack of rollback netcode and lack of cross-platform play on launch, leaving players hopeful that the team at Koei Tecmo will take their feedback into consideration for its next DoA title.

item.title: As the dust settles on PlayStation's announcement it's ditched a new game from Hideo Kojima, analysts are now discussing why Sony may have walked away.
item.description:
As the dust settles on PlayStation's bombshell announcement that it has ditched Physint, an ambitious-sounding next-gen project from legendary Metal Gear Solid creator Hideo Kojima, analysts are now discussing why Sony may have walked away.
Physint will, of course, remain in production — though now backed by PlayStation's archrival Xbox, in a significant and much-needed PR win for Microsoft's gaming division.
Sony, meanwhile, is being seen as backtracking on yet another big public moment — this time, the enthusiastic handshake between PlayStation Studios boss Herman Hulst and Kojima that heralded Physint's announcement — even as fan complaints continue over PlayStation's disc-killing initiative, and disquiet over the shutdown of Destiny 2 development.
Why risk further backlash? For Dr. Serkan Toto, CEO of Japanese games industry consultancy firm Kantan Games, sales of Kojima's most recent title Death Stranding 2: On the Beach may be to blame.
"Kojima games have a strong platform marketing halo effect and are not about sales alone, but it seems the steep drop-off from DS1 to DS2 spooked Sony enough to cut him off," Toto wrote in a post on X/Twitter this morning.
Direct comparison between Death Stranding 1 and 2 is difficult as official sales for the latter were never announced by Sony or Kojima Productions "This is of course not a good sign," Toto noted, speaking to IGN.
Today, a fresh sales estimate from Alinea Analytics has pegged Death Stranding 2 at 2.5 million copies. This is a far cry from the number of players who tried the original Death Stranding — around 20 million, but there are caveats here.
Here's what we know for certain: that Death Stranding 1 had sold 5 million copies by March 2021, and had 20 million players by March 2025 — a figure that includes those who accessed the game via subscription services like Xbox Game Pass, or who claimed it free via Epic Game Store promotions. In July this year, Kojima Productions stated that the Death Stranding franchise had reached a cumulative 27 million players across both games.
Sales analysis, again from Alinea, suggests that Death Stranding 2 sales have now slowed to a trickle, that several notable discounts on the game have failed to move the needle, and that revenue for the game remains lower than that of its predecessor.
The picture that emerges here is one of a sequel that failed to build upon or even match the sales and reach established by Death Stranding 1. Perhaps this was enough to "spook" Sony, as Toto suggested, especially as both projects feel like lavish productions, with lengthy development cycles and Hollywood stars in key roles.
Looking ahead to Physint, it's possible Sony felt that the juice needed to fund a similar production scale and length was simply not worth the squeeze — especially as Physint looks to be even more ambitious, with yet more famous actors involved. Last year, Kojima estimated the game was still 5-6 years from completion, and there have been teases that some form of movie production is also involved.
All of these issues will now be Microsoft's to solve, though as Toto noted, the financial costs involved will be balanced somewhat by the positive impact this news has for Xbox as a brand, especially after a summer of layoffs, studio closures, and its own set of project cancelations to focus on games more likely to move the needle. While Physint may still be half a decade away, it is now a marquee title (and potential console exclusive) for Xbox's next-gen Project Helix.
"This doesn’t look great for PlayStation among core gamers," noted Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliot today. "Especially right now. From a strictly financial perspective, though, I can understand Sony’s position. In a vacuum, anyway.
"Ballpark math: word on the street is that the first Death Stranding cost about $100 million to make, and the second somewhere in the $150 million – $200 million ballpark (longer dev cycle, COVID, and all that)," he continued. "Depending on marketing overhead and the opportunity cost of pulling those Guerrilla developers onto DS1, the franchise has almost certainly broken even – but not by much.
"Margins are the name of the game now," Elliot added, suggesting that recent key misses from PlayStation Studios have made the company more cautious over which big-budget projects it backs. "Over the past few years, scares like Concord (cancelled, $300 million+ down the drain) and softer sales from the likes of Marathon (1.8M sold), Saros ($61M), Marvel Tokon (725K, $49M), and Lego Horizon Adventures (under 250K across Steam and PS5, $11M) seem to be making PlayStation more wary."
But while ditching Kojima will likely save many further millions, the optics of losing such a prestige project are uncomfortable at best, especially after the recent online ruptions over Bungie and physical media. "The PR miss of Xbox scoring off Sony’s stumbles could have been avoided," Elliot noted. And, as The Game Business' Christopher Dring noted on X/Twitter today: "You don't sign a Kojima game for the profit margin. It's a credibility play. Strong win for Xbox."
Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

item.title: Pre-orders went live for Grand Theft Auto 6's new PS5 controllers this morning and the experience was extremely chaotic.
item.description:
Preorders went live for Grand Theft Auto 6's new PS5 controllers this morning, and the experience was extremely chaotic.
As you might expect, there's a ravenous demand for anything related to GTA 6. When Sony announced that it'd be opening up preorders for a pair of limited edition GTA 6-themed PS5 controllers last week, it was a safe bet that there'd be scalpers, store errors, and other disruptions in abundance — and that's exactly what happened when preorders opened this morning.
I got into a queue on PlayStation's online store half an hour before preorders began, and once the flood gates were opened, I was kicked to the back the line with an hour-plus wait time. Thankfully, that time was quickly cut in half, likely from people unwilling to wait that long and leaving the queue, but even then, I still had issues. PlayStation's website kept giving me an error when I tried to sign into my account, forcing me to open the store in a new browser on another device. Eventually, I got through, but it was friction I could've done without.
So far, the controllers appear to be selling out at various retailers, though there is still some availability at the time of writing. GameStop and Best Buy are sold out of the white controller, while Target and Amazon appear to have them stock. Meanwhile, the black controller is exclusive to PlayStation Direct and appears to still be availabile.
PlayStation has implemented a system where users can only purchase one controller per account, which will likely limit some scalping, but not eradicate the issue. The controllers are currently being resold for nearly double the price on eBay, though it remains to be seen if people will actually buy them. It's unclear how long these controllers will remain in stock and if there will be a restock if they sell out.
With the release of preorders for the controller, we are just a little over two months away from the release of Grand Theft Auto 6. Marketing is in full swing now, though it's unclear what will come next. Will there be another trailer for the game following the expansive, in-depth gameplay reveal? Will Rockstar talk about GTA Online before release? There are still a lot of questions, but at least we are in the endgame.
Grand Theft Auto 6 will release on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.
Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

item.title: Pokémon cards will likely be used as currency following a global apocalypse, one venture capitalist has suggested.
item.description:
Pokémon cards will likely be used as currency following a global apocalypse, one venture capitalist has suggested.
Pete Levin, founder of VC firm Griffin Gaming Partners, said that the "global phenomenon" of Pokémon trading cards was perfect for use as a new form of currency, should the world's current economy collapse due to some terrible catastrophe.
Levin claims to manage more than $1.6 billion of gaming assets and, handily, also happens to be the owner of some 500,000 trading cards. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter, he explained that Pokémon cards remained a hugely profitable asset for collectors — and suggested that their worth would also be kept, at least to some degree, even after the nukes fall.
"Pokémon is a global phenomenon," Levin said. "I'm absolutely convinced that if the world suffered an apocalypse tomorrow, the following day the global currency would be Pokémon cards.
"Pokémon cards are beating the S&P 500 by 3,000%," he continued. "Emanating from Japan, it really took hold around the world in the late '90s and early 2000s. It then had a zenith moment and then a nadir moment, and ever since then, it's been on a parabolic growth curve. And that really has driven the international market expansion for trading cards."
Despite being poised to personally profit if we all started to use Charizards instead of loose change, Levin also pointed to a few other reasons he was confident in his prophecy.
For one, card grading companies such as PSA now standardize card quality ratings and provide proof of authenticity. With these, cards have a clearly quantifiable value — even if the price attached to that is left for the market to decide. Then there's the so-called "kidult" phenomenon, where adults now make up around 30% of global toy sales — a figure that's on the rise.
"You've got a generation that has come of age that is nostalgic for these toys, for these vintage video games, for these trading cards and comic books, and they now have disposable income," Levin concluded. "So that's also been a huge tangible driver in the market."
So, never mind the claim that there's a greater than 10% chance AI will end civilization in the next 10 years. If you've got a couple of Pikachu Illustrators in your back pocket, you may still be able to buy a few tins of beans.
Word that we should all begin hoarding Pokémon cards for use after the apocalypse will likely not help ongoing issues with Pokémon card scarcity, which has prompted U.S. retailer Target to begin slicing open boxes to deter scalpers. In Japan, some releases are being limited to Japanese residents only, while facial recognition for adults and children has been rolled out in some locations to limit daily card purchases.
Pokémon cards have become a prime target for scalpers and thieves over the past few years due to their soaring popularity and the perceived value of rare cards. New card releases frequently sell out completely, and The Pokémon Company has appeared unable or unwilling to fully keep up with demand — despite a staggering 10 billion cards printed last year alone.
Looking to start your collection? We've also got a list of the 10 most expensive Pokémon cards of 2026 so far, and a first look at Mega Evolution's Delta Reign expansion, set to release in November this year.

item.title: What's stopping the animation from being implemented throughout Samsung's launcher is that the permissions necessary for that only exist in Android's background processes.
item.description:
Apple just announced iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, yesterday at its "Suprise and Shine" event. Though the concept of a foldable is new for Apple, it's entering into a vast, existing landscape of folding phones. So of course someone has already recreated the Duo's neat opening animation on an Android phone.
While the iPhone Duo doesn't come out until October 23, one of the more interesting early features shown off has been the Apple A20 Pro's ability to power both displays at the same time. This allows the Duo to have an opening and closing animation that makes it look, at a certain angle, like the phone's display is expanding. The effect is unique to Apple's new phone, but a software developer on Reddit was able to recreate it on a Galaxy Z Fold, though it isn't exactly system wide.
In the video user moomanjohnny shared to the GalaxyFold subreddit, you can see the Galaxy Z Fold 8's outer display fade out as the phone opens, only to have the inner display take the image of the home screen and expand it once the phone is fully opened. This was done by taking data from the hinge sensor and then creating a transition animation using a screenshot of the homescreen – not exactly ready for system-wide implementation.
What's stopping this from being implemented throughout Samsung's launcher is that the permissions necessary for that only exist in Android's background processes. Later in the thread, moomanjohnny explains, "SystemUI is privileged by the system in the way that it can layer itself on top of apps, and tell other apps how to render. SystemUI receives a list of surfaces and can composite them on the screen where it wants using SurfaceFlinger." That because it's a security risk. "Unfortunately, as far as I'm aware, no vendor has made any of these APIs available to anything other than SystemUI."
It's up in the air whether or not this kind of opening animation will ever be supported on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it's clear that the hardware capability is there. With how the Samsung Mobile Twitter page threw a fit about the iPhone Duo during Apple's event, it's possible that this functionality will find its way to the Samsung Fold range at some point.
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

item.title: Wardogs, a new all-out warfare FPS game that has been blowing up on Steam, is officially coming to consoles... but it will be a while.
item.description:
Wardogs, a new all-out warfare FPS game that has been blowing up on Steam, is officially coming to consoles... but it'll be a while.
As part of its launch, the team behind Wardogs, Bulkhead, confirmed that it will bring the massive shooter to consoles. The game is slated to arrive on Xbox and PS5 in 2028, but is available in early access on Steam starting today. The game is launching for $39.99, with plans to increase the price as the game expands. The idea is to reward fans who support the game in its earliest stages and not charge them a full $60–$70 for an unfinished product.
“Wardogs is ambitious, rough around the edges and still has a long way to go, but that is exactly what Early Access should be,” said Joe Brammer, CEO at Bulkhead. “We’re putting the game in players’ hands, listening to what they tell us and taking the risks needed to turn it into something that can last. More than anything, we want people to get online, talk to each other and have the kind of fun in an FPS that we grew up having.”
All of this suggests that Wardogs might be targeting 2028 for its 1.0 release, as PlayStation is extremely selective about early access titles on its platform, unlike Xbox. Major titles like Subnautica 2 have had to skip PS5 during early access, but there have been exceptions. However, I wouldn't hold my breath for Wardogs being one of those exceptions at the moment.
It's also interesting that Bulkhead specifically confirmed PS5 as a release platform, since PlayStation 6 is heavily speculated to release next year. Whether the game will also have a native PS6 version remains to be seen, but would presumably be playable on the next-gen console with backward compatibility should that be a supported feature.
Wardogs is one of the most surprising titles of 2026, as it really only emerged over the summer as marketing began to ramp up. However, the response from players who participated in playtests has been glowing and indicates the shooter space may have another big contender going forward.
Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

item.title: Robert Downey, Jr.'s Doctor Doom will wear at least two costumes in Avengers: Doomsday, and a new action figure gives us a much better look at his alternate suit of armor.
item.description:
Robert Downey, Jr.'s Iron Man rarely stuck to just one suit of armor in his many MCU appearances, and it appears that the same will hold true for Downey's new character, Doctor Doom. Doom will wear at least two distinct suits of armor in Avengers: Doomsday, and now we've gotten a much better look at his secondary costume thanks to a new Hot Toys figure.
Having already revealed their standard Doctor Doom figure, Hot Toys and Sideshow Collectibles have now debuted the companion Victor von Doom figure. Get a closer look in the slideshow gallery below:
While this armor follows the same traditional Doom design aesthetic (green cloak and metal mask), it's quite a bit different from the other Doom suit seen in the film. It seems to be less an actual suit of armor and more a piece of regal formal wear. The green suit is more muted in color and completely covers up the armored components here. The mask is also completely different - smoother and less aggressive than the one on the Doctor Doom armor.
This suit appears to be the same one Downey's character was wearing during his initial appearance in the post-credits scene of The Fantastic Four: First Steps. Our best guess is that Doom will wear this suit in the early portions of Avengers: Doomsday, before his true power and motivations are made clear to Earth's Mightiest Heroes.
Sideshow hasn't yet put the Victor von Doom figure up for preorder. But if the Doctor Doom figure is any indication, we'd expect it to cost around $285 and release in late 2027.
Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18. Fans can get an early tease for the movie in the form of Avengers: Endgame Encore, which is set to be the longest MCU movie to date. Marvel also teased Doomsday by recreating the trailer in LEGO form.
Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky.

item.title: The senior director of Call of Duty's anti-cheat system has explained why Activision shadow bans players instead of outright permanently banning them from the game.
item.description:
The senior director of Call of Duty's anti-cheat system has explained why Activision shadow bans players instead of outright permanently banning them from the game.
For years, there has been a lot of friction regarding cheating and the implementation of anti-cheat in major games like Call of Duty. Anti-cheat in gaming isn't perfect; it makes mistakes and accidentally bans people who shouldn't be banned, it can create headaches around launching the game with things like Secure Boot, and some players are placed in ambiguous "limited matchmaking" pools, a.k.a. shadow banned.
There has been a lot of mystery over how anti-cheat works, so IGN spoke with Call of Duty's senior director of game security, David Andrews, to learn a bit more about its Ricochet anti-cheat. In our exclusive interview, I asked why Activision opts to shadow ban players suspected of cheating rather than simply outright banning them there and then.
"We have limited matchmaking that we will put a suspicious account into to isolate them while other checks are either running or we're waiting on other data," said Andrews. "We're kind of doing this review process of looking at that account more holistically and seeing what's really going on here. It's kind of this stopgap measure to immediately remove them without making it be permanent [or without creating] irrevocable impact to that account and to that player, giving us some breathing room to figure out what is going on with this account and then either restoring them to the player population because it was kind of a false alarm situation."
Andrews went on to note that Activision has a variety of ways to deal with suspected cheaters, but uses techniques such as shadow banning to potentially rehabilitate a player and allow them the chance to keep playing without issue.
"We have also done some rehabilitation through the limited matchmaking saying, 'Hey, you can't do that behavior that you've just been engaged in and you can come back if you stop,' or whatever. We have a lot of enforcement capabilities. We have limited matchmaking, we have ranked play bans, we've got remote play bans, we've got temporary and permanent account suspensions, we've got hardware bans. We can do all kinds of things, and each time we're dealing with a particular style or type of cheating, we're sort of evaluating which one of these kind of makes sense for this group of cheaters. Can they be rehabilitated? Are we ultimately 100% confident in this? Is more research required? Whatever the case might be, we'll figure out what to do that's appropriate."
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 drops next month and Infinity Ward aims to be receptive to player feedback. Anti-cheat is a big part of the optics of a Call of Duty game, and the team tested Ricochet's MW4 implementation during the recent beta. It did result in an accidental ban of a former pro player, but Call of Duty's comms team rectified the issue and confirmed it was a mistake.
Call of Duty has a reputation for cheating, especially with the free-to-download battle royale Warzone. Activision has spent a significant amount of time, money, and energy in response, even taking on cheat makers in court, although it, like all video game developers, faces an uphill battle in the war on cheaters.
Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

item.title: A Professor Layton and the Curious Village remake has been announced by series developer Level-5.
item.description:
A Professor Layton and the Curious Village remake has been announced by series developer Level-5.
Revealed today during the Level-5 Vision 2026 Showcase, this fresh version of the classic puzzle game will arrive at some point in 2027 for Nintendo Switch, Switch 2, PC via Steam and PlayStation 5.
A press release notes that the remake's characters have been reimagined in 3D, while the world of St. Mystere has been made more immersive with greater depth and richer detail. Professor Layton and the Curious Village's animated cutscenes have also been given a lick of paint, with higher resolution and widescreen formatting.
🆕 Annonce – Professeur Layton et l’étrange village Remake sortira sur Nintendo Switch 2 et Nintendo Switch en 2027, découvrez la première bande-annonce du jeu. pic.twitter.com/cuhbyIpMbH
Next year will mark the 20th anniversary of Professor Layton and the Curious Village's original release back on Nintendo DS, kickstarting a series that now extends to two trilogies of games featuring Professor Hershel Layton and his apprentice Luke Triton, plus further spinoffs and a memorable crossover with Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney.
An all-new Professor Layton game is also on the way, of course: Professor Layton and the New World of Steam, which is set to launch for Switch, Switch, PC and PS5 on December 10.
Will further remakes follow? That may depend on how well Professor Layton and the Curious Village performs. But for anyone wanting to see how the series started on modern hardware, this remake may end up well worth a look.
Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

item.title: Fans are reacting to the announcement of a unique "Customer Appreciation" sale that Nintendo claims has been "made possible in part by tariff-related refunds."
item.description:
Fans are reacting to the announcement of a unique "Customer Appreciation" sale that Nintendo claims has been "made possible in part by tariff-related refunds."
Nintendo will temporarily reduce the price of "dozens of Nintendo Switch digital games and bundles, plus savings on select physical games, downloadable content, accessories, amiibo and apparel." Whether Nintendo Switch 2 games will also be included is unknown.
While cheaper prices are nothing to be sniffed at, the framing of this promotion — which runs for just two weeks, from September 13 through September 26 — as being funded by tariff refunds has certainly raised eyebrows.
Nintendo and numerous other companies are now recouping the money they previously handed over to the US government as part of tariffs that have since been deemed illegal. Nintendo (and again, numerous other companies) raised prices to combat these tariffs, and fans have been calling for Nintendo to pass some of its tariff refund back to gamers. Indeed, a proposed class action lawsuit is brewing, calling for Nintendo to share its refund with Switch purchasers — but the company itself has argued that it has no reason to do so.
Today's sale announcement is being taken by some fans as a way to placate those fans who remain upset about all this, while also continuing to signal that it won't be doling out partial refunds to any recent Switch and Switch 2 customers.
While the lack of partial refunds isn't particularly surprising, what is rather remarkable here is the acknowledgement that Nintendo did very well out of the whole situation — to the extent that it is now lowering prices (by a small amount, on a selection of titles, for a limited time).
"Ah yes, because they couldn't have possibly had a sale if it wasn't for the tariffs," wrote one fan on video game forum ResetEra.
"It's a coupon. Makes them look good and gets people to spend money. Win-win for them," wrote another.
"Lol the gall of them," wrote a third. "'We'll do a sale to celebrate not giving your money back.'"
"Nintendo is f***ing allergic to any percentage higher than 30%," wrote yet another fan. "Still, the fact that they're offering a discount at all as some sort of 'apology' is surprising in itself."
Nintendo is yet to reveal exactly which games and other products will be part of the sale, and we may not find out until the price reductions go live on September 13. But even despite the scepticism, there are plenty of fans who have already expressed excitement for the sale, and who sound ready to splash out further.
"So you get your tariff money back... if you give them more money," concluded one fan. "You know what? I'll take it lol."
Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

item.title: Nintendo announces a 30% off Customer Appreciation Sale for Switch games and accessories, funded in part by tariff refunds following recent US litigation.
item.description:
Nintendo has announced a new 'Customer Appreciation' Sale in the US, offering 30% off dozens of Switch games and more, starting on September 13 and running through September 26.
Select games, downloadable content, accessories, amiibo, and apparel will be discounted, although Nintendo has not yet provided a full list of the games and other products that will be included in the sale across the Nintendo eShop, Nintendo Store, and other participating retailers.
The video game giant has also said that the promotion is "made possible in part by tariff-related refunds." The company says it "absorbed most tariff-related costs," but the refunds have helped make promotions such as this new sale possible.
Nintendo previously faced questions over what it would do with money returned after the US tariff regime was challenged. Nintendo recently raised the prices of some Switch products globally, citing a combination of factors including tariffs, rising component costs, labor and shipping.
It subsequently argued that consumers were not entitled to refunds for purchases made at those higher prices after a court ruled the tariffs illegal. Nintendo said customers had received "exactly what they bargained and paid for" and that it was not required to retroactively adjust prices following the outcome of the tariff litigation.
Nintendo also maintained that it had absorbed the tariff costs on the Switch 2 itself rather than simply passing them directly on to consumers.
Now, however, Nintendo says tariff-related refunds have helped make its latest promotion possible. It's fair to say fan reaction to the sale announcement has been... mixed.
But it's already been a fairly big week for Nintendo fans. With the two Nintendo Directs back-to-back, preorders for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Metroid Ravenous going live, as well as that elusive 40th Anniversary Zelda Switch 2 announcement.
Nintendo has also just released a fresh firmware update for its Switch and Switch 2 consoles, including adding VRR support while playing Switch 2 in TV mode.
You can usually find Robert lost in open-world RPG games like Elden Ring and Cyberpunk 2077. Outside of gaming, his passions include reading comics (especially Superman, Batman, and Spider-Man), taking photos, and keeping up with the latest in film and TV.
His primary coverage focuses on tracking down the best gaming deals and diving into the fast-paced world of Trading Card Games (TCGs). He regularly covers everything from the latest releases in Pokémon TCG and the most expensive cards to comprehensive Magic: The Gathering buying guides. As a massive Doctor Who fan, he also keeps a close eye on physical media deals like Doctor Who Blu-ray preorders, and occasionally steps away from commerce to contribute reviews for the site, such as his review of Doctor Who's latest season.

item.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake's divisive character models may reflect Shigeru Miyamoto's love of puppetry, one Nintendo veteran believes.
item.description:
This week’s Zelda Direct finally revealed gameplay for the Ocarina of Time remake. But while the reveal triggered a wave of nostalgia for the 1998 original N64 game, the remake’s art style divided opinion. The new character designs, in particular for Link, came under particular scrutiny.
Weighing in on the topic on Twitter / X, Nintendo veteran Takaya Imamura suggested the new character models may reflect developer legend Shigeru Miyamoto’s love of puppetry.
“What I felt upon seeing this character model (of Link) is that Miyamoto-san’s love of puppet dramas (ningyogeki) is strongly reflected here too!” Imamura said. His opinion is worth considering — Imamura worked at Nintendo for over 30 years, particularly on the Star Fox and F-Zero series, and of course, was the art director for Ocarina of Time’s sequel, The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask.
It’s important to note that Imamura is just speculating here (as he clarified in a follow-up post) on the inspiration behind the Ocarina of Time remake’s character designs. However, Miyamoto’s love of puppets is well-known, and the use of their aesthetics can be seen across other Nintendo series and promotions. Let’s look at some possible inspirations behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s character models.
Aside from Japan’s traditional bunraku puppet theatre, Japanese broadcasters have produced many TV series featuring puppets, particularly in the 1960s and 70s. For example, national broadcaster NHK’s archives under the “ningyogeki” genre category bring up a whole page featuring short clips from puppet TV shows spanning from the 1950s to the present day. Other TV stations got in on the act as well. Japan also imported puppet series including Gerry Anderson’s Thunderbirds, which acquired an enduring fanbase and influence on anime.
Link’s new look seems to be a call back to the whimsy and nostalgia of such TV series (and in keeping with the classic game itself). But some commenters were quick to notice that Ocarina of Time remake’s sharp-nosed, big-eyed characters also bear a strong resemblance to more recent Japanese puppet TV series. Specifically, NHK’s The New Three Musketeers (Shin Sanjushi, 2009-2010), not to mention the 2014 puppet version of Sherlock Holmes. The puppets for The Three Musketeers adaptation were made by legendary Japanese puppet maker Studio Nova, which also made the physical dolls that were used to create Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined’s character models.
Analyzing the new character designs for the Ocarina of Time remake has seen commenters sharing their own comparisons to classic puppet series and movies. The oversized, plastic-looking eyes and prominent facial features have reminded some of 1982 fantasy classic The Dark Crystal (and its more recent Netflix prequel).
Of course, Nintendo fans will have spotted Miyamoto’s fondness for puppets before now. For example, the Star Fox characters strongly resemble The Muppets in style, with actual puppets being used in the TV ad campaign for the series’ very first game back in 1993 (Time Extension).
And who can forget all the puppets used in Nintendo’s 2015 E3 presentation? The game company went all out, teaming up with The Jim Henson company (of The Muppets fame). Miyamoto, then Nintendo America president Reggie Fils-Aimé, and late Nintendo Japan president Satoru Iwata, among others, were all transformed into Muppet-like puppets.
At the time, Fils-Aimé talked to IGN about Miyamoto’s love of puppets. “One of the things that he shared was that in his youth, he used to make puppets," he said. "So that led to a series of brainstorms and it led to our little collaboration with Henson studios and creating the Nintendo muppets. It was a very fun collaboration.”
A remake of such a beloved classic like The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time was always going to please some fans and leave others wanting. What do you think of the new character designs?
Are marionette models a good fit for Hyrule or do the sharp-nosed, doll-like faces put you off? Let us know in the comments.
Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

item.title: IGN exclusively reveals Hour Zero, a new four-part live-action prequel miniseries for Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve starring Josh Holloway and Brandon Routh.
item.description:
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, the latest entry of the long-running flight simulation combat series from Bandai Namco, is hitting PCs and consoles next month. But before players get their hands on the game, IGN can exclusively reveal that a live-action prequel miniseries starring Lost’s Josh Holloway and Superman Returns’ Brandon Routh will be available to stream later this month.
The trailer for Hour Zero, which you can see in the player above, shows Holloway, Routh, and Cobra Kai’s Tamlyn Tomita as “three strangers who survive the opening days of the Republic of Sotoa's invasion of the Federation of Central Usea,” according to the series’ official description.
Holloway stars as “a pilot with nowhere to land,” Routh plays a “doctor who saved his enemy,” and Tomita portrays a “news anchor silenced for telling the truth.” Bandai Namco says the characters’ stories “set the stage for the narrative players will experience in the deep, engaging Campaign Mode in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.”
I spoke to Holloway ahead of the show’s launch about jumping into the cockpit and joining the Ace Combat universe. Holloway says that acting in the series reignited his love of gaming.
“When I was younger, I was a gamer,” Holloway says. “Ms. Pac-Man, Centipede, Galaga. I went away from gaming for many, many years, and this has gotten me addicted. It's so real and so visceral. Layering a story onto this game really raises the stakes. After playing the game, I could feel myself in that cockpit because I got to do it in the studio. So now I have that sense memory while I'm playing the game, which is a blast.”
Holloway says that getting to participate in the action scenes of Hour Zero fulfilled one of his lifelong dreams, dating all the way back to before Top Gun was on the big screen.
“God, my first fantasy about being a fighter pilot was [the 1970s World War II fighter pilot TV series] Baa Baa Black Sheep. Remember that? That just tore my imagination up. When I was in high school, I looked into how I could become a fighter pilot. [But] you have to be a fricking math genius for them to let you in the hundred million dollar plane. That dashed my dreams of actually being a fighter pilot. [But I thought,] Aha, I can still be an actor. For me, being a fighter pilot is right up there with being a cowboy.”
Holloway, who appeared in the 2007 game Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars, says that he’s not particularly keen on revisiting performance capture in another video game, but is up for adapting more games for the big screen.
“I'm less interested in being a part of the video game world. [Instead,] I'd like to turn one of those into a movie. I feel like there's room in the Ace Combat world to possibly make a feature. Same thing with cowboy[s]. I do want to do that. I've looked at Red Dead Redemption. It's not just a game anymore. They're like real simulators with real stories.”
Holloway, who’s had the chance to play through Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve ahead of the game’s public release, says there’s one major tip he has for anyone who decides to dive in on October 2.
“Be aggressive,” Holloway says. “If I start to chill out, I got somebody locked on my tail already. So you’ve got to be like, ‘Oh my God, I'm going for it,’ and just hammer down.”
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve will be available in early access for Deluxe Edition holders on September 29 and launch for all players on October 2. The game is available now for preorder on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC via Steam.
Michael Peyton is the Senior Editorial Director of Events & Entertainment at IGN, leading entertainment content and coverage of tentpole events including IGN Live, San Diego Comic Con, gamescom, and IGN Fan Fest. He's spent 20 years working in the games and entertainment industry, and his adventures have taken him everywhere from the Oscars to Japan to Buenos Aires, Argentina. Follow him on Bluesky @MichaelPeyton

item.title: We asked the directors about physical media, how they chose the finale's subtitle, and more.
item.description:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation is the finale of Square Enix's ambitious project that began with FFVII Remake in 2020 and continued with FFVII Rebirth in 2024. A full trilogy that retells and remixes the story and world of one of the most beloved video games of all time is a crazy idea on paper, but in less than a year, it will be complete. IGN recently went hands-on with Revelation — you can read Michael Higham's preview coverage for his in-depth thoughts — and after playing for roughly two hours for myself, I sat down with two of the creators responsible for bringing this saga to a satisfying conclusion: Director Naoki Hamaguchi and Battle Director Teruki Endo.
I asked the pair (through an interpreter) about how they're keeping the third entry fresh, both with small adjustments to the combat system and new events in areas we already visited in Rebirth. But I was most fascinated to learn about Square Enix's approach to wrapping up this saga: How did they choose a subtitle for this all-important finale? What has this team learned from releasing three AAA RPGs in the span of eight years? And, how does Hamaguchi feel about Revelation releasing on a PlayStation 5 disc in Sony's final year of producing physical games? Read on to learn about all of this and more, including how Fortnite of all things inspired Revelation in one key way.
IGN: Thank you both so much for meeting with me. I appreciate the time. I played about two hours of Final Fantasy VII Revelation yesterday, and I really liked it. And something I'm most interested in is that there are new areas in Revelation, but a lot of it is the same map as Rebirth. I'm curious about the team's process for revisiting old areas and adding interesting content to differentiate them from how they appeared in Rebirth.
Naoki Hamaguchi: So I will say that all the various side quests and side contents that are going to be appearing in FFVII Revelation, those are going to be completely new. And with the meteor looming in the sky over the planet, there are a lot of, I guess, seismic shifts that have occurred because of the meteor approaching. So there are various geographical changes that you'll be able to see in the existing areas from Rebirth. So even though they are continuously appearing from various games, it is going to look a little bit different from the previous game.
But in terms of how the actual gameplay and the exploration might feel different from Rebirth is that when we were making Rebirth, the focus was on the open world aspect of the game. So we wanted to introduce a lot of large, vast areas that offered the horizontal width in terms of how big the area is going to look like. With FFVII Revelation, we want to take it a step above. So in addition to the horizontal width, we're now adding a vertical depth that allows players to explore using the Highwind or the Chocobo. So both of these modes of transportation allow you to fly and jump high in the air and things like that. So it does give you a more expanded feel of how the open world is going to look like in the world of the FFVII Remake series. So in that sense, even with the preexisting areas appearing in FFVII Revelation, the way you might approach, the way you might explore, and the way it feels when you explore these areas might feel different from FFVII Rebirth.
IGN: I did like the Highwind a lot, and being able to skydive down into different areas and steer where I landed. It indicates there will be a lot of freedom in how you re-explore areas. And I'm wondering if there were challenges in developing what appears to be a game that's maybe more freeform than Rebirth in how you can tackle objectives.
Hamaguchi: So this kind of ties into the first question that you had, but one of the goals that we had as a development team is to kind of expand as we step into the next installment. So from Remake to Rebirth and from Rebirth to Revelation, we wanted to take a step above. So from the evolution from going from Rebirth and then heading into Revelation was that again, “How can we expand the open world?” And the way we achieved that is to achieve this planetary exploration, the open world map scale where players can just really just explore the entire planet using the Highwind. So taking on that challenge was one of the rather difficult parts of the development for sure.
So the idea of the party parachuting down from the Highwind was something that we had pretty early on in the development of FFVII revelation. When you look at the original release of FFVII, the way it worked was that the Highwind would just land directly onto the ground and the characters would just exit out of the ship. But if we were to do that in this very high fidelity open world, we’d need to think of how the geography would work out in the map. So we needed designed surfaces where it would make sense for the Highwind to be able to smoothly land, if that makes sense. But that wasn't really realistic for us to consider. So that's why we had this parachuting idea. And when you look at other games, specifically like Fortnite, it did seem that players, modern audiences, were pretty familiar or welcome to this idea of characters flying down the air using parachutes. So I thought it would be a fun way to also introduce a seamless transition from the air to the ground. And I think the end result turned out well for us. I'm really happy with how that is in the game.
IGN: As exploration has evolved, combat has evolved in each new entry as well. In Revelation, there's a version of classes, fighting on Chocobos, and other tweaks. How did you decide what elements to stack on the combat system previously established in Remake and evolved in Rebirth?
Teruki Endo: We as a team felt that the combat system was in a perfect state with FFVII Rebirth. So while we did think about, “What can we do to add more?”, we couldn't really find any areas that needed to be improved, if that makes sense. I feel like it was in pretty good state already. So because of that, rather than coming up with ideas of how we can change something, it was more about expanding what we already had, because again, we felt that the combat system we had in Rebirth was already really good and in a perfected, complete state. So the idea was more about, “How can we offer more flexibility for customization and freedom to players?” So that's kind of the approach that we had, and how we came with the ideas of the FITS system and the Chocobos engaging in combat.
IGN: Would it be fair to say one of the themes of Revelation from a gameplay perspective is freedom? I think about the Highwind’s exploration, and then what you just said about the combat. Was that kind of a core idea of this game?
Hamaguchi: I think yes, but one of the very big concepts that we had for this game is resolve. So resolve being the core theme of the game, that doesn't only just apply to the story or the characters, it also applies to the overall game experience that the players will have when they play FFVII Revelation. So the idea is that we want the players to make the choice themselves. We're going to offer them a lot of different options and choices and they can choose to control or play as Cloud, but they can also choose to play as the different party members in this game as well. So that's one example.
The other example when you look at combat is that we're giving them the FITS system. So they have four choices there as well. So again, it's not just about the story, it's not just about the combat system, it's about the overall game experience. We're offering them a wide array or a diverse range of options that the players will be able to choose from. And this is something that was also offered in the original FFVII as well. So one of the goals definitely was to recreate that experience through FFVII Revelation.
And we kind of showed a glimpse of this in the State of Play stream, but in certain side quests players will have the choice of which character they would play as. So in the State of Play stream, it showed that players can either choose to play as Vincent or choose to play as Cid. In scenarios like that, depending on the character you go with, the conclusion of the side quest or the way the story plays out could change drastically. So again, that's also another example of the player choices that we're offering for the game experience. All in all, players will be faced with these chances, opportunities where they get to make these choices so that each and every player might have a very unique experience depending on the choices that they made throughout the game.
IGN: So, resolve is a focus of the game. I can't help but notice that word starts with R-E. Was Resolve seriously considered as a subtitle for this game, or were there any other words that start with "re-" that you were considering?
Hamaguchi: [Laughs] So to answer the first question, “Resolve” was actually not considered as one of the contenders for the title, and there actually is a reason for that. The development team that we have for this game is in Japan and consists of Japanese staff. So when we were having internal discussions about what the core concept or the philosophy of this game was going to be, we did use the term “resolve,” but in Japanese. So in Japanese, the word is called “ketsui,” which as you can tell, doesn't have that "re-" sound. And then when we were making plans for our first major reveal at Summer Game Fest earlier this year, I actually wrote a script for myself on stage, and I did want to use the term for ketsui, resolve. So when I was looking at the English equivalent of that, I found out that resolve actually started with RE, so I thought, “Oh, this is actually a perfect fit!”
I can talk more about how we ended up with the title Revelation. So way before this whole resolve discussion that we had, we did decide to go with the title Revelation, but even before we made that decision, there were actually three final contenders and I had a discussion with the creative director of the series, Tetsuya Nomura.
In terms of the other two contenders that we had aside from Revelation, I might share it sometime in the future, but I don't think now is the right time for us to share it because the game isn’t out yet. If we do share the other two contenders, I don't want people to be like, "Oh, the other one was better than Revelation." And it feels like it's just going to create some unnecessary discussion and debates online. So I feel like now's not the right time. Maybe sometime down the line we might be able to revisit this discussion again and share what the title could have been. But I will say that when I discussed with the North American Square Enix team, I did share the other two options that we had as the final contenders, and we unanimously agreed that Revelation was the best choice. So I think we made the right decision on that.
IGN: Okay, I'll ask you again in a couple of years what the other two were.
IGN: I'd like to talk a little bit more about the combat because Vincent quickly became my go-to character during the preview. And I know you've talked about Vincent a little bit before, but what's maybe your favorite detail that’s gone unnoticed about Vincent's combat style so far?
Endo: I don't think this is something that I can say as something that was unnoticed because I actually addressed this myself during the PAX West stage panel that we had yesterday. But one of my personal favorite functions of Vincent's combat design is that I was able to implement this feature of him being able to turn into the Galian Beast anytime during combat. Just to hold R1 and be able to revert back to human form and go back to the Galian Beast form anytime during combat. Having that in the game, I think that's actually my personal favorite. I'm really glad I was able to do that.
And one of the big reasons why I wanted to implement that was because when you look at the existing party of playable characters, we already have a lot of different options, a lot of different characters that each has its own unique combat experience. So people who have already played Remake and Rebirth might already have their own favorite character to play in combat. So in order for us to deliver a very impactful gameplay experience for these new characters, we needed to make sure that there's something very unique and different about them. So considering that, if we were to follow suit with the original and have this function where Vincent is only able to turn into the Galian Beast only under a specific condition, I don't think that would've been the best way to go about it with the FFVII Remake series. So I think I made the right choice to do that.
So when you think about it, Vincent being able to switch back and forth between his human form and the Galian Beast form, it's essentially two characters packed into one because each form has its own unique movesets and motions as well. So the animation artist had a bit of an extra hard time compared to the other characters trying to implement all these motions into the combat. So in that sense, I think we spent a lot more effort and time developing Vincent's combat system.
IGN: I do want to ask, Revelation is coming out in the last year that Sony is producing physical PlayStation discs, and it is launching with a physical edition. And Final Fantasy VII has this rich history with PlayStation. Was it important to you to have this game release on a physical disc?
Hamaguchi: Last week with the State of Play announcement, we tied it to the preorder as well. So right after the State of Play, the preorders launched. But before we arrived at that decision, there were a lot of internal discussions and back and forth amongst myself and other internal staff members in terms of how we should treat or handle the physical editions. And this whole disc discussion, it is a rather sensitive issue, and I don't think a lot of the media has asked us about this so far. So I would like to discuss how we approached it.
First and foremost, personally, I'm very happy that we are able to release a physical disc version of FFVII Revelation considering how the entire gaming market, or the landscape, is veering towards the disc-less direction. And after we launched preorders, we did see some fans voicing their concerns and raising questions about the physical discs requiring some internet download. So I would like to address that.
When we had an internal discussion with the development team about how we wanted to approach the physical discs and the physical releases of FFVII Revelation, initially there were conversations about using the same disc size as we did for, say, FFVII Rebirth. But if we were to do that, it would mean that we would have to make a compromise in terms of the fidelity and the quality of the game. So as a development team, we didn't want to do that. We didn't want to make any compromises for the game. So realistically, the only choice that we had was to release this physical disc, but with certain sections of the game being a digital download format through the physical disc. With that being said, I completely understand that not all players might be happy with this decision, but at the same time, I am happy that we were still able to release a physical format of the game. So I am quite satisfied with the end results as well. I would hope that our fans and players would be able to share that as well.
IGN: I think it's impressive that you've released a whole trilogy in the span of roughly eight years. That's rare in the video game industry these days. So I'm wondering if there are any learnings from this major project and its development that you can take with you as you move on to whatever's next.
Hamaguchi: I will say that the top priority for us as a team right now is to put a full focus on completing the development of FFVII Revelation. So in terms of what we would do as the next work or the next game, we haven't really put that much of a thought into it right now. That said, looking at the overall landscape and environment of game development, it does seem like creating and developing these AAA titles, it just takes longer and longer as it goes by. So considering that, having this consistent team that's stuck together throughout the last 10 to 12 years, creating the entire trilogy, and being able to gather all this knowledge and experience that can be applied to future development, I think we were in a very lucky position to be able to do that.
But yeah, we are very much eager to utilize and leverage the experiences that we have made throughout these years of development of the FFVII Remake series. I would say it's undecided in terms of the direction that we're going to after the completion of the Remake series, but we hope the fans and players will look forward to what we work on next. But to reiterate our top priority, our full focus is on FFVII Revelation right now. So until we actually complete it and ensure that it's the intended quality that the game should be, I don't think we will have any actual ideas of what we're going to work on next.
IGN: Thank you both so much for your time, and good luck the rest of the way with Revelation. We're looking forward to it.
Hamaguchi and Endo: Thank you.
Parts of this interview were edited for clarity.
Logan Plant is the host of Nintendo Voice Chat and IGN's Senior Editor, Playlist and DB. The Legend of Zelda is his favorite video game franchise of all time, and he is patiently awaiting the day Nintendo announces a brand new F-Zero. You can find new episodes of NVC every Friday on the IGN Games YouTube channel, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app.

item.title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi has offered an explanation for why the physical disc version of the game on PlayStation 5 and Xbox requires a download to play.
item.description:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi has offered an explanation for why the physical disc version of the game on PlayStation 5 and Xbox requires a download to play.
Earlier this month it emerged that the physical version of Final Fantasy VII Revelation on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X comes on a single disc and requires an internet connection to download other parts of the game. The first two games in the Final Fantasy VII remake trilogy, Remake and Rebirth, come on two discs: one for installation and one for play. Switch 2 owners get Final Fantasy VII Revelation on a game-key card.
This sparked a backlash among some fans who had hoped for Final Fantasy VII Revelation to be playable without an update, like its predecessors in the long-running franchise. “The game not getting a proper physical release on any platform is the only detail that should be discussed,” commented X / Twitter account Does it play?, which advocates for physical media and has campaigned for video game preservation. “What were you thinking, in all honesty?”
In a new interview with IGN, Hamaguchi suggested that even if Square Enix released Revelation on the same number of discs as Rebirth, it would still have had to “compromise” on the quality of the game. So, the "only choice" it had was to release the game on a single disc with a forced download to play.
“First and foremost, personally, I'm very happy that we are able to release a physical disc version of FFVII Revelation considering how the entire gaming market, or the landscape, is veering towards the disc-less direction,” Hamaguchi said, referencing Sony’s controversial decision to end production of PlayStation discs from 2028.
“And after we launched preorders, we did see some fans voicing their concerns and raising questions about the physical discs requiring some internet download. So I would like to address that.
“When we had an internal discussion with the development team about how we wanted to approach the physical discs and the physical releases of FFVII Revelation, initially there were conversations about using the same disc size as we did for, say, FFVII Rebirth. But if we were to do that, it would mean that we would have to make a compromise in terms of the fidelity and the quality of the game. So as a development team, we didn't want to do that. We didn't want to make any compromises for the game. So realistically, the only choice that we had was to release this physical disc, but with certain sections of the game being a digital download format through the physical disc.”
Hamaguchi went on to acknowledge fan complaints around this, but insisted he’s happy with where Square Enix ended up on the issue.
“With that being said, I completely understand that not all players might be happy with this decision, but at the same time, I am happy that we were still able to release a physical format of the game,” he said. “So I am quite satisfied with the end results as well. I would hope that our fans and players would be able to share that as well.”
Final Fantasy VII Revelation is due out across PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and Nintendo Switch 2, on April 8, 2027.

item.title: Project Zeta is a mashup of multiple live-service genres, but for developer Nirvanana, it’s best described as an “espresso MOBA.”
item.description:
Project Zeta is a mashup of multiple live-service genres, but for developer Nirvanana, it’s best described as an “espresso MOBA.”
This four-teams-of-three ‘Tactical Hero Arena’ third-person action game is, essentially, a race involving as many teamfights as possible. The game actively encourages teams to fight each other, scrapping over objectives throughout each phase of a session. MOBAs typically focus combat down lanes, but in Project Zeta, around three minutes into each session, the focus becomes fighting over objectives. You have to seek out teamfights to win. This is not a game about hiding in bushes.
Each session is made up of seven phases. The first phase sees players defeat ordinary monsters to level up — all very MOBA. It’s a warmup phase meant to give players breathing room to develop a strategy. Generally, you’re on the hunt for prisms, which drop from prism bosses. Grab one then take it to one of the ballasts in the center of the map to score a point. The first team to score five points wins, exiting the game in first place.
“What we're aiming to deliver is a removal of the lane-ing in traditional MOBAs,” Nirvanana CEO Namseok Kim told me at gamescom 2026. “It's objective-driven with a lot of teamfights. So that compressed experience is what we're looking for. As fans of the MOBA genre, we believe that the fun of MOBAs comes from playing smart and winning the teamfights. And we need it so that you can enjoy an endless supply of that kind of experience in the compressed 20-minute time of a session. It's going to be a very dense experience. So we wanted to propose a new kind of MOBA.”
Another unique aspect of Project Zeta is its lack of a crosshair at the center of the screen, which you typically see in hero shooters and 3D MOBAs. This means basic attacks always land. More accurate aim does not factor into fights; instead, the idea is that success comes from your understanding of the each hero's abilities, mind games, and positioning. Combat is a sort of dance between dodging enemy attacks and making sure your attacks land.
Reducing downtime, players in eliminated teams are immediately revived with their cooldowns and HP restored. Battle royale MOBAs typically restrict players to a limited number of lives, so players play passively in order to survive. Project Zeta has a score race with unlimited respawns and a quick time-to-kill. The game wants players to take risks to eliminate other teams, and because everything is restored once a team is eliminated, the hope is that players won’t shy away from getting into scraps.
“We wanted the sessions to feel like a Formula 1 race,” Namseok Kim said. “Everyone is racing toward these objectives. That is what Project Zeta is.”
Like a racing game, Project Zeta displays a scoreboard on the top left that fluctuates as teams turn prisms in. “Everything needs to happen in 20 minutes,” Namseok Kim explained. “So everything that makes a MOBA fun is compressed into that short time. Yesterday, one journalist said that if other MOBAs are coffee, then Project Zeta could be like instant espresso. And we agreed, that was a great analogy. We had made up the term ‘multi-team tactical arena’ to describe Project Zeta, but personally I like ‘espresso MOBA’ better.”
Namseok Kim said that one of the reasons he made Project Zeta is because his daughter thought a game of Riot Games’ League of Legends took too long. “There's too much to learn,” he said. “There's too much to memorize. And I played League of Legends with her 10 times and every time she didn't like it. I made Project Zeta to help her approach MOBAs, and I think that would maybe make the concept accessible.”
It’s also worth noting that Project Zeta was built from the ground up to be playable on a controller, with the goal that PC and console players can compete on a level playing field. There’s also an auto-itemization scheme. Outside of a session, you can set up your skills in advance to focus more on aggression, support, or defense, and then when you enter a session, Project Zeta will automatically purchase the necessary skills for you.
Reinforcing the focus on quickfire combat, Project Zeta has no pure tankers or pure healers. “Personally, I think pure tankers and pure healers are kind of boring!” Namseok Kim said. “And if we had these kinds of characters, it drastically increases the time-to-kill. And if you have a longer time-to-kill, in a session, the third team that joins is usually the most advantageous because A and B are already engaged in combat. And even if A… they won, if their HP is already low, they're tired. And if the third team comes in, they're probably going to have the upper hand. In order to guarantee the proactiveness of a multi-team, we have to have a short time-to-kill. And that's why we don't have pure tankers or pure healers.”
The question for Nirvanana, of course, is will Project Zeta have enough of a pull to drag MOBA fans away from their current favorite game. Will players ditch League of Legends or Dota 2, for example, to give it a try, at a time when most video game companies are finding it increasingly difficult to make a dent in the established players? The fast-paced nature of the game, its streamlined design, and its availability on console may help it stand out.
Project Zeta, developed by Nirvanana Studio and published by PUBG company Krafton, is currently confirmed for PC via Steam and PlayStation 5.
